issue.issue_text: Whether the decision to conduct a search under sub-section (1) of Section 30 of the 1994 Act must be a collective decision of the Appropriate Authority, or if a decision by an individual member, such as its Chairman, is legally valid.

facts: A search was conducted at the appellant's clinic based on allegations of illegal sex determination under the 1994 Act.
The Appropriate Authority for the district was a three-member body consisting of the Civil Surgeon (Chairman), the District Program Officer, and the District Attorney.
The decision to conduct the search was made solely by the Civil Surgeon in his capacity as the Chairman.
The other two members of the Appropriate Authority were not part of the decision-making process.
The Civil Surgeon cited urgency as the reason for acting alone.
law: Section 30(1) of the 1994 Act grants the power to search a clinic to the 'Appropriate Authority'.
This power can only be exercised if the 'Appropriate Authority' has a 'reason to believe' that an offense has been or is being committed.
The requirement for the 'Appropriate Authority' to have a 'reason to believe' acts as a safeguard against arbitrary searches.
The law specifies that if a particular thing must be done in a particular manner, it must be done in that manner only.
application: The Court interpreted the term 'Appropriate Authority' in Section 30(1) to mean the collective body, not its individual members acting alone.
It reasoned that the decision to authorize a search, a drastic action, must be a collective decision of all members of the Authority.
A decision made by a single member, even the Chairman, does not constitute a decision of the 'Appropriate Authority' as required by the statute.
The Court rejected the excuse of urgency, noting that the members could have been consulted quickly through methods like video conferencing.
Since the decision was made by the Civil Surgeon alone, it was contrary to the procedure mandated by law and therefore completely illegal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the decision to conduct a search under Section 30(1) of the 1994 Act must be a collective decision of the Appropriate Authority. A decision made by an individual member, such as the Chairman, is legally invalid. Consequently, the search in this case was illegal, and the subsequent prosecution based on it was quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether a prosecution, based entirely on evidence and material seized during a search that is found to be illegal, amounts to an abuse of the process of law and should be quashed.

facts: A search and raid were conducted on the appellant's clinic on April 27, 2017, under the Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994.

The 'Appropriate Authority' for the district, which was legally required to authorize such a search, was a three-member body consisting of the Civil Surgeon, the District Program Officer, and the District Attorney.
However, the decision to authorize and conduct the raid was made solely by the Civil Surgeon, who was the Chairman, without the involvement or decision of the other two members.
An FIR and a complaint were filed against the appellant, and the prosecution's case was based entirely on the material and evidence seized during this raid.
There was no other evidence connecting the accused to the alleged offence apart from what was found in the search.
law: Under Section 30(1) of the 1994 Act, a search can only be authorized if the 'Appropriate Authority' has 'reason to believe' that an offence has been or is being committed.
The decision to take action under Section 30(1), such as authorizing a search, must be made by the 'Appropriate Authority' as a collective body, not by one of its individual members.
A decision made by an individual member, even the Chairman, is not a valid decision of the 'Appropriate Authority' and renders any subsequent action, like a search, illegal.
application: The Court applied the law to the facts and found that since the decision to conduct the search was made by the Civil Surgeon alone, it was not a valid decision by the 'Appropriate Authority'.
Because the proper legal procedure was not followed, the Court declared that the search itself was "entirely illegal" and "vitiated".
The Court then examined the basis of the prosecution and noted that the FIR and complaint were founded exclusively on the material seized during this illegal search.
The Court reasoned that allowing a prosecution to continue when its entire foundation is evidence obtained from an illegal act constitutes an abuse of the legal process.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the search was illegal and the prosecution was based entirely on evidence seized during that illegal search, continuing with the prosecution would be an abuse of the process of law. Therefore, the Court accepted the issue and quashed the FIR and the complaint against the appellant.

cases.case_name: Aslam Mohammad Merchant v. Competent Authority & Ors.
cases.principle: Whenever a statute provides for a “reason to believe”, either the reasons should appear on the face of the notice or they must be available on the materials which had been placed before the authority.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The interpretation of the statutory expression "reason to believe" is contextual and depends on the specific legislation; the test is whether a reasonable person, under the circumstances, would be propelled to take action, and this standard cannot be construed in a manner that creates a procedural roadblock which would frustrate the object of the statute.
obiter: Under Section 26 of the Indian Penal Code, a person is said to have "reason to believe" a thing if they have sufficient cause to believe that thing and not otherwise.

It is a trite law that whenever a statute provides for “reason to believe”, either the reasons should appear on the face of the notice or they must be available on the materials which had been placed before the authority.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The decision to conduct a search under sub-section (1) of Section 30 of the 1994 Act must be a collective decision of the Appropriate Authority, not an individual member. A search conducted based on the decision of an individual, even the Chairman, is illegal and vitiates the entire action. Consequently, a prosecution based entirely on material seized during such an illegal search is an abuse of the process of law and must be quashed.
legal_tests_applied: The test for whether an authority has 'reason to believe' is whether a reasonable man, under the circumstances placed before him, would be propelled to take action under the statute.
policy_considerations: Section 30 is a very drastic provision, and the condition that the Appropriate Authority must have 'reason to believe' serves as a safeguard against arbitrary search and seizure actions.

While the object of the 1994 Act requires that action not be delayed by procedural roadblocks, this does not eliminate the fundamental requirement that the decision to act must be made by the Appropriate Authority as a body, not by its individual members.
Continuing a prosecution that is founded entirely on evidence gathered during an illegal search amounts to an abuse of the process of law.
